promptText: Why can't a RAG system's answers be evaluated with simple exact-match unit tests the way a deterministic Java method would be tested?
options: Because LLMs cannot produce string output at all
Because an LLM generates free-form text and the same correct meaning can be phrased countless different ways, so there is no single fixed 'correct string' to assert equality against
Because unit tests are incompatible with any HTTP-based API
Because exact-match tests are too slow to ever run in CI
explanation: RAG systems are instead evaluated statistically — metrics scored per example and aggregated into a pass rate or average across a representative test set, with an agreed threshold, analogous to accuracy thresholds in classical ML testing.

promptText: What is the key difference between Context Precision and Context Recall in RAG evaluation?
options: They are two names for the exact same metric

Context Precision measures how much of what was retrieved was actually relevant (noise vs. signal); Context Recall measures how much of all relevant information that exists in the corpus was actually retrieved
Context Precision only applies to sparse retrieval, Context Recall only to dense retrieval
Context Precision is always higher than Context Recall by mathematical necessity
explanation: Precision is about noise in what you got back; recall is about blind spots — whether the corpus's relevant information was actually surfaced. Low recall means retrieval missed something generation can never recover.

promptText: Why is 'faithfulness' NOT the same thing as 'factual correctness' in RAG evaluation?
options: Faithfulness is always computed using BLEU, while correctness uses ROUGE

Faithfulness only asks whether a claim is supported by the retrieved context, saying nothing about whether that context itself is true — a model can be perfectly faithful to a stale or wrong document and still be factually wrong in the real world
Faithfulness and factual correctness are interchangeable terms with no meaningful difference
Faithfulness can only be measured by human annotators, never by an LLM judge
explanation: Conflating the two is called out as one of the most consequential mistakes in RAG evaluation — corpus quality (freshness, accuracy) must be evaluated as its own separate concern from faithfulness.

promptText: Why do BLEU and ROUGE correlate poorly with human judgment on open-ended, free-form generation tasks?
options: They only measure surface lexical (n-gram) overlap, not meaning, so a correct paraphrase scores poorly while a wrong answer sharing many surface words can score deceptively high
They can only be computed on documents longer than 1000 words
They were designed exclusively for image captioning, not text
They require a working internet connection to compute
explanation: 'The cat sat on the mat' and 'A feline rested upon the rug' mean nearly the same thing but share almost no n-grams — a correct, differently-phrased RAG answer can score poorly on BLEU/ROUGE despite being helpful and accurate.

promptText: Mechanically, how does a well-built LLM-as-judge faithfulness evaluator typically score an answer, rather than judging it holistically as one blob?
options: It asks the judge to rate the whole answer 1-10 in a single pass with no further structure

It decomposes the answer into individual atomic claims, verifies each claim against the retrieved context with a narrow true/false-style judgment, then aggregates the ratio of supported claims to total claims
It compares the answer only against a human-written reference using edit distance
It counts the number of words in the answer and penalizes anything over 200 words
explanation: Narrow, per-claim judgments are more reliable than one holistic judgment because they reduce the judge's susceptibility to being swayed by fluency or tangential correctness; the final score is supported claims / total claims.

promptText: Why must a RAG failure be diagnosed by decomposing it into retrieval vs. generation stages rather than relying on a single end-to-end accuracy score?
options: Because end-to-end accuracy cannot be computed for any AI system

Because the two failure modes demand completely different fixes — a retrieval failure needs chunking/embedding/reranking fixes while a generation failure needs prompt/model fixes, and a blended score cannot tell them apart, risking wasted engineering effort on the wrong fix
Because generation failures never actually occur in production RAG systems
Because retrieval and generation always fail together or not at all
explanation: This is analogous to debugging a slow HTTP endpoint without distinguishing 'the database query is slow' from 'the serialization is slow' — per-stage instrumentation is required to know where to spend effort.

promptText: What is the key practical difference between reference-based and reference-free evaluation metrics?
options: Reference-based metrics are always faster to compute than reference-free ones

Reference-based metrics require a pre-written 'gold' answer to compare against, while reference-free metrics check internal consistency (e.g., does the answer follow from context) and thus can run on live production traffic where no gold answer exists
Reference-free metrics can only be used for sparse retrieval evaluation
There is no practical difference; both require identical setup
explanation: The practical takeaway is to build a small, high-quality reference-based golden set for offline regression testing, and rely on reference-free metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance) for continuous production monitoring.

promptText: Why does NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) discount a relevant document's contribution logarithmically by its rank position?
options: Because logarithms are computationally cheaper than linear functions

Because a relevant document at rank 1 is worth more than the same document at rank 10, since a reranker or top-k cutoff may never let a low-ranked chunk reach the generator at all — the log discount models this real attention/inclusion pattern
Because NDCG only applies to documents ranked below position 10
Because logarithmic discounting eliminates the need for an IDCG normalization step
explanation: The log2(i+1) denominator discounts relevant items more heavily the further down they sit, matching the real effect where low-ranked chunks may be truncated before ever reaching the generator.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend using a stronger, separately-budgeted model as the LLM judge rather than reusing the same model that generated the answer?
options: Because using two different models always doubles inference cost with no benefit

Because a model is prone to rating its own output favorably (self-preference bias), and errors it systematically makes as a generator it will often fail to catch as a judge for the same underlying reason
Because judge models must always be smaller than generator models by regulation
Because Spring AI technically forbids using the same ChatModel for both roles
explanation: Self-bias is a documented LLM-as-judge failure mode; using a separately-budgeted, often stronger judge model reduces this risk, since judge quality corrupts every downstream decision made from its scores if wrong.

promptText: What does BERTScore do differently from BLEU/ROUGE that lets it capture paraphrase and synonym equivalence?
options: It counts overlapping 5-grams instead of 4-grams

It embeds candidate and reference tokens with a pretrained transformer and matches tokens by embedding similarity rather than exact string match, so 'purchased' can correctly match 'bought' despite sharing zero characters
It requires human annotators to manually align every word pair
It ignores word order entirely and only counts vocabulary overlap
explanation: BERTScore computes precision/recall/F1 using soft embedding-similarity matches between tokens rather than hard string overlap, though it remains a reference-based metric requiring a gold answer.

promptText: A team's BERTScore numbers are consistently above 0.95, yet engineers still find obviously wrong answers in manual review. What is the most likely explanation?
options: BERTScore is being computed on the wrong programming language's tokenizer

Embedding-similarity metrics can be fooled by topical overlap — two answers sharing the same entities and vocabulary embed close together even when they disagree on a critical detail like a wrong number or inverted comparison
The evaluation harness has a bug that always returns 0.95 regardless of input
BERTScore cannot be computed for RAG-generated text at all
explanation: High BERTScore confirms 'this answer is about the right topic,' not 'this answer is correct' — it should be paired with an LLM-judge faithfulness check that can reason about specific claims, not relied on alone for high-stakes correctness.

promptText: A team's offline faithfulness dashboard has shown a stable 92% score for months, yet real customer complaints about wrong answers are rising. What does this discrepancy most likely indicate?
options: The judge model has run out of available tokens and is silently failing closed

The evaluation golden set has calcified and no longer represents production traffic — user behavior, the corpus, or the model provider may have drifted, and it's also possible faithfulness is being preserved against an increasingly stale or incorrect corpus, which faithfulness scoring alone would not detect
Faithfulness scores are mathematically incapable of ever moving, regardless of underlying changes
This pattern proves the LLM judge itself has been compromised by prompt injection
explanation: This is the textbook 'eval set doesn't generalize to production' failure; the fix is refreshing the golden set from a fresh, unbiased production sample and checking for a corpus-quality regression that faithfulness scoring alone wouldn't catch (faithfulness vs. correctness gap).

promptText: Why is 'overfitting the golden set' a real risk in RAG evaluation, and what is the recommended mitigation?
options: It is not a real risk since LLMs cannot memorize test sets the way classical ML models can

If engineers iteratively patch each golden-set failure individually, the system starts memorizing the test set's specific phrasings rather than improving general quality; the mitigation is holding out a portion of the golden set that is never used for iteration, only for final validation
The only mitigation is deleting the golden set entirely after each release
Overfitting only applies to embedding models, never to prompt engineering
explanation: This is the classical ML overfitting problem reborn in prompt engineering; a held-out validation subset that is never used to drive iteration protects against a system that looks great on the visible test set but hasn't generalized.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend against gating a summarization feature purely on ROUGE-L in CI, even though it is fast, free, and deterministic?
options: ROUGE-L cannot be computed for text longer than one paragraph

ROUGE-L cannot distinguish a genuinely good paraphrase-heavy summary from a bad one, cannot detect hallucinated facts not present in the source, and can be gamed by a model that copies more source phrasing verbatim — the recommended approach is a tiered gate using ROUGE-L as a cheap tripwire and an LLM-judge check as the actual quality gate
ROUGE-L requires a live internet connection to compute, making CI unreliable
ROUGE-L only works for machine translation tasks, never summarization
explanation: The chapter explicitly recommends a tiered strategy: cheap lexical metrics as fast, free tripwires on every commit, with the more expensive and accurate LLM-judge metrics reserved as the actual quality gate at a less frequent cadence.

promptText: Why does the chapter warn that tying compensation, launch decisions, or team OKRs directly to a single eval score is an organizational risk, not just an academic one?
options: Because eval scores are always randomly generated and carry no real signal

Because it creates a structural incentive (Goodhart's Law: 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure') to tune the system or even the eval prompts themselves to that specific metric rather than to genuine quality
Because compensation can never legally be tied to any technical metric
Because eval scores are proprietary and cannot be shared with leadership
explanation: Mitigations include rotating/refreshing golden sets, holding out validation subsets, and pairing automated scores with periodic human review before high-stakes launch decisions, to guard against gaming the metric rather than improving real quality.
